title: China's GB/T 34336 Standard for Aerogel Insulation: What It Actually Tests and How to Read a Supplier's Test Report
content:
Most global buyers evaluating silica aerogel blankets know the familiar Western references — ASTM C518 for heat flow meter measurements, ISO documents for hydrophobicity — but far fewer know that China, now the world's largest aerogel manufacturing base, runs its own national product standard: GB/T 34336-2017, "Reinforced nanoporous aerogel products for thermal insulation" (纳米孔气凝胶复合绝热制品). If you source aerogel blankets, felts, or panels from Chinese suppliers — which most large-volume buyers now do — this is the document behind the numbers on their datasheets. Understanding what it requires, and what it deliberately does not cover, is one of the fastest ways to separate a serious manufacturer from a trading company relabeling generic felt.

What GB/T 34336-2017 actually is

The standard was issued on 14 October 2017 and took effect on 1 September 2018. It is a recommended national standard (the "T" in GB/T), classified under Q25 — thermal insulation, sound absorption, and lightweight fireproof materials. Its scope covers reinforced nanoporous aerogel composite products for building and industrial thermal insulation, and it specifies terminology, classification, requirements, test methods, inspection rules, marking, packaging, transport, and storage. Notably, the standard itself states it can serve as a reference for other aerogel product types, which is why you will see it cited even for product forms it does not explicitly define.

In practice, Chinese manufacturers typically declare conformance to a grade within the standard — grade A being the more demanding tier — and grade affects the numeric limits on thermal conductivity, density tolerance, and mass loss.

The properties it requires — and the test methods behind them

Published third-party test reports from Chinese aerogel blanket producers give a realistic picture of what a GB/T 34336 grade A conformance table looks like, and which national test methods are invoked for each property:

  • Thermal conductivity: measured to GB/T 10294-2008 (the Chinese protected hot plate method, functionally the counterpart of ASTM C177). Commonly declared limits are ≤0.021 W/(m·K) at a 25°C mean temperature and ≤0.036 W/(m·K) at a 300°C mean temperature for grade A blankets.
  • Density: tolerance within ±20% of the declared value — a check aimed at consistency of production, not at an absolute number.
  • Compression recovery: typically ≥90%, reflecting the blanket's ability to spring back after being compressed during wrapping or cladding.
  • Tensile strength: tested per GB/T 17911 (the standard for refractory ceramic fiber products), with horizontal and vertical requirements around 200 kPa in published conforming reports — a property that matters enormously for installation handling.
  • Vibration mass loss: ≤1.0%, a dusting and shedding check that speaks directly to the fiber-shedding complaints installers raise with poor-quality blankets.
  • Permanent linear change: after 24 hours at 650°C, shrinkage must stay within roughly -2.0%, which is the standard's proxy for high-temperature dimensional stability.

Three things to check when a supplier sends you a "GB/T 34336 compliant" report

First, look at the mean temperature attached to every conductivity value. A report showing 0.020 W/(m·K) means little unless it says at which mean temperature the measurement was taken — Chinese datasheets conventionally report both a ~25°C value and an elevated-temperature value (often 300°C), and the gap between those two numbers is itself a quality signal. A blanket whose conductivity rises steeply between 25°C and 300°C likely has a fiber matrix or opacifier loading that underperforms at process temperatures.

Second, check the test method number, not just the result. GB/T 10294 (hot plate, steady-state) and GB/T 10295 (heat flow meter) give slightly different answers, and some suppliers mix results from different methods in one table. If a report cites no method at all, treat every number in it as marketing.

Third, compare the reported density against the datasheet's declared density. Because the standard allows a ±20% band, a nominally "192 kg/m³" blanket testing at 210 kg/m³ is still conforming — but heavier than specified, which changes your pipe support loading and your installed cost per square meter.

Where the standard stops — and where buyer diligence must start

GB/T 34336 is a product standard: it defines what a conforming aerogel product is. It does not tell you how the material will behave in your specific service. Chinese industry commentary — including reports from securities analysts and industry associations reviewing the domestic market — consistently points out that in-service failures with aerogel insulation are rarely about the blanket failing its lab tests. They involve system design: water ingress through failed cladding, compression at pipe supports where the blanket is crushed beyond its recovery limit, mechanical damage during installation, and wrong thickness selection for the actual surface temperature. China's design-side engineering code for industrial insulation (the GB 50264 series on design of insulation for industrial equipment and piping) governs those decisions, and experienced Chinese EPC contractors treat product conformity and design conformity as two separate gates.

There is also a building-versus-industrial split worth knowing. The same product standard covers both markets, but building projects in China are additionally steered by fire-classification and energy-code requirements — the frequently cited "A1 non-combustible" rating of silica aerogel blankets is a separate fire test result, not something GB/T 34336 alone confers. If fire performance is part of your specification, ask for the fire test report by its own standard number.

Why this matters for global buyers

China's aerogel industry has scaled faster than any other region's, and most Chinese producers have parallel test data under both GB/T and ASTM/ISO methods. When you receive a quotation, asking for a full GB/T 34336 conformance table — every property, every test method number, every mean temperature — costs you nothing and gives you a sharper screening tool than a marketing datasheet. Suppliers who can produce that table from an independent lab, with dates and sample IDs, are the ones running a real QC loop; the rest are selling felt.
